fact: In September 1868 Tom Allen was arrested and put under £1,000 bonds, which ended the planned fight with Joe Goss.
In December 1868 Tom Allen was arrested in Cleveland for violating the prize-fighting laws, and the court held that training for a prize fight was not a violation of state law, so he was discharged.
On 14 May 1869 Tom Allen was arrested in Cincinnati for training for a prize fight in Ohio, gave bonds not to fight in Ohio within a year, and was released to go back to training.

In June 1869 Referee Val McKinney swore that Sherman Thurston and Billy Carroll offered to let him name his price to decide a fight for them; Carroll offered $100 to any man who would say he had offered to bribe McKinney, and Thurston, Carroll, B. Riley and James Stewart swore counter-affidavits; the stakes stayed with the men holding them under legal process.
In 1870 a sheriff and his deputies broke up the Allen-Goss fight, and the fighters fled to an adjoining county.
In February 1870 John Williams sued Tom Kehoe and Mike McCoole, the stakeholders of a $30 bet on the proposed Allen-Gallagher fight, and the court gave judgment for the defendants.
After their 1869 fight, Tom Allen sued to recover his stake money, and in April 1870 he and Mike McCoole compromised their claims to the excursion money, McCoole taking $1,232.50 and Allen $1,000.

On 1 November 1870 Tom Allen was arrested on the steamboat Belle Ida and held in the calaboose; a planned Allen-Gallagher fight set for that Tuesday was spoiled by police interference. Daniel B. Stephens petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, Judge Stewart of the Court of Criminal Correction attached Chief of Police James McDonough for contempt, and McDonough surrendered Allen to the court, which discharged him with no charges made against him. Allen's lawyer, Mr. Voullaire, said a report that Allen would sue the city for false imprisonment was untrue.
In early November 1870 a fight was arranged in secret so the police would not be told, and was held early in the morning.

In June 1871 Tom Allen was in Jem Mace's party at Wyandotte when Sheriff William Holcomb tried to capture them, and they were not taken; a rumour had Allen with Mace at Pleasant Hill, where the sheriff and deputies hunted for him.

On 20 May 1872 Nelson Adams died of a pistol wound from the accidental discharge of a pistol in Tom Allen's hands at Allen's saloon at 417 Washington Avenue; Allen ran for a physician and called the police.
Tom Allen's fights with Mike McCoole near St. Louis were indirectly responsible for the Missouri boxing statute of 1873, which made prize fighting a felony.

On 1 August 1873 Tom Allen was tried in the Court of Criminal Correction on a charge of assault to kill after Joseph P. Moore said Allen struck and kicked him in Allen's saloon; the judge discharged Allen on the evidence, and police officers were present to testify to his character but were not needed.
On 16 August 1873 Tom Allen was a witness for the defense in the Mollie McCoole case in Police Court.

On 21 and 22 September 1873 Tom Allen and Mike McCoole were arrested by detectives and released on $1,000 bonds each to keep the peace in Missouri for three months, the bonds being signed by John Whelan and William Brown for Allen and McCoole.

On 25 September 1873 Maj. Jones offered Tom Allen as a witness to prove that Mike McCoole was too sick to appear in James Scott's $900 debt suit in Judge Knight's court, St. Louis; the case was continued.

In October 1873 a Madison County, Illinois, writ ordered the sheriff to take Tom Allen and others to the circuit court at Edwardsville to answer an indictment for prize-fighting in the Allen-McCoole fight, returnable 3 November; in November Gov. Beveridge of Illinois issued requisitions for Allen, McCoole and others engaged in the September fight.

On 28 October 1873 John Renshaw of St. Clair County swore that Tom Allen and Ben Hogan were about to fight in Illinois and asked for warrants; on 29 October Illinois Gov. Beveridge sent Col. E. L. Higgins with a hundred stands of arms to East St. Louis to prevent the Allen-Hogan fight.
Allen said he could not fight in Missouri because of the bonds.

On 21 November 1873 Tom Allen and Arthur Chambers were arrested by St. Louis detectives on an Illinois requisition for the prize fight with Mike McCoole and held without bail at the Four Courts; on 28 November Allen put up $3,000 in greenbacks as collateral for the Illinois bail bond that freed Chambers.

Police Chief McDonough meant to push the Wash Home case against Tom Allen and his associates, but on 9 December 1873 Allen, Johnnie Smith, Sam Smith and Jim Eagan were discharged in Police Court over their Sunday chase after Ben Hogan.
On 24 January 1874 the Missouri governor signed the bill suppressing prize-fighting, which the Republic said dimmed Tom Allen's hopes in Missouri.
A man believed to be part of a watch swindle was seen entering Tom Allen's saloon in January 1875, and three men recently from Baltimore were arrested in a boarding house nearby.

Tom Allen, Jack Looney, Arthur Chambers, Dublin Tricks and Tom Kelley were discharged from their bond to answer a Madison County indictment at Belleville on January 30, 1875, because of a flaw in the indictment.
Tom Allen telegraphed Harry Hill in May 1875 about Rooke's $1,500 share of the stakes, and Rooke's backer threatened Hill with a suit for it.
Jack Madden was arrested in Tom Allen's saloon on suspicion of a robbery on December 26, 1875, and was released after a search at the Third Precinct Station.
Tom Allen was indicted in Kentucky in 1876 for prize fighting in the Goss fight.
Ned Donnelly had a constable attach Tom Allen's saloon outfit and trunks on April 11-12, 1876, over a $125 claim against Allen.
Ned Donnelly sued Tom Allen before Justice Walther on May 1, 1876, for $125, and the hearing was postponed to the next afternoon.
Tom Allen and Joe Goss were bound over before Squire Anthony to keep the peace in Ohio for one year in May 1876.
Thomas Hackett of St. Louis garnished Tom Allen's stake money, held by A. F. Edwards, over a debt Allen had run up in St. Louis, in August 1876.
At the request of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, Prosecuting Attorney Baker made Joe Goss and Tom Allen give bonds to keep the peace in Ohio for one year in August 1876.
Tom Allen and Joe Goss were arrested after their September 7, 1876 fight in Kentucky, and Allen was held at Newport.
Tom Allen was released on bail of $3,000 in Covington, Kentucky, on September 11, 1876, after the Goss fight, with Farrell sureties.
In September 1876 Tom Allen said he had attached the stakes from the Goss fight the night of the fight, and he planned to sue in Ohio rather than Kentucky.
Tom Allen fled to Windsor, Ontario, in November 1876 to avoid prosecution, was arrested in Chicago on Kentucky officers' request, and failed to appear for trial on November 20, 1876.
Tom Allen stayed in Canada to avoid the Kentucky warrants, and City Marshal Boland of Covington met him in Toronto on February 20, 1877.
The Farrell brothers, sureties on Tom Allen's $3,000 bail bond, had their property near Covington, Kentucky, levied on in March 1877.
Mayor McLean of East St. Louis revived an old indictment against Tom Allen for inducing a ring encounter in East St. Louis in March 1883.
Tom Allen was tried in the St. Louis Police Court on October 30, 1883, for keeping a disorderly house at his saloon, and was discharged.

Tom Allen was arrested at his Market Street saloon on February 9, 1884, at the instance of W. P. Farrell of Covington, Kentucky, on a Kentucky requisition, after Farrell's money demands; he gave a $2,000 bond with two sureties, and on February 13 Judge Noonan released him, with the Prosecuting Attorney saying he would not press the matter.

On February 21, 1884, Judge Chester H. Krum asked Gov. Crittenden of Missouri to refuse to surrender Tom Allen on Kentucky's requisition, arguing it was meant to enforce a debt Allen owed to Farrell; Crittenden said he was not prepared to honor it and would consider it well first.
Frank Rush was shot in front of Tom Allen's saloon at 621 Market Street at about 1 a.m. on December 22, 1884, by an unknown man who escaped.

Tom Allen, Flint's second, was arrested on April 18, 1888 under a Franklin County warrant charging him with aiding and abetting the McManus-Flint prize fight, and gave a $500 bond to appear before Justice Frazee at Union the next morning.
Tom Allen was indicted by the Franklin County grand jury in connection with the Flint-McManus fight, and renewed his bond before Judge Noonan on May 19, 1888.

Tom Allen and Charley Daly were taken to the police station and released on bond after a Sunday-morning street fight on June 17, 1888; the Police Court case against Allen was continued at his request, and on June 21 Allen, Daly and John Ryan were tried on counter charges of disturbing the peace, when Judge Cady fined Allen $10.
Judge Cady fined John Ryan $15 on Tom Allen's charge of malicious trespass on July 20, 1888.

Tom Allen sued Bill Clark, the final stakeholder in the Daly-McManus match, on December 7, 1888, for the $1,000 he had deposited with him, with interest and costs; a second count said Clark had received a sum from the Globe Printing Co. for Allen and had not paid it.

A St. Louis County warrant issued by Justice Caffrey named Tom Allen for prize fighting at the Kelly-McManus fight at Florissant, and Allen was arrested on the afternoon of February 11, 1889 and gave bond.

Lincoln County, Mo., Sheriff Jessie Coomes came to St. Louis on September 5, 1889 seeking the arrest of Tom Allen and others for prize fighting at Troy; the defendants were arrested in St. Louis by detectives, and each was held in a $500 bond for his appearance.

James St. John reported his watch and chain stolen on January 20, 1890 and Tom Allen notified police; Thomas Barrett and George Ohls were arrested on a corner near Allen's saloon, and on January 21 a petit larceny warrant was sworn out against Barrett after St. John identified his watch.
Edward Reilly said Tom Allen, a saloon-keeper and prize-fighter on Market Street, slugged him without provocation on October 12, 1890, leaving him with severe head injuries.
John Craig was charged in the First District Police Court with disturbing Tom Allen's peace, and Judge Morris discharged him on June 24, 1891.
Tom Allen said on November 1, 1893 that he would try to get bail bonds for the jailed Sharpe and was willing to put up a cash guarantee.
Police arrested a suspect calling himself John Foley at Tom Allen's saloon on Market Street on March 8, 1894, after a witness pointed him out as one of the robbers of a Broadway saloon.

Patrick Sullivan and Charles Dempsey picked a fight with Tom Allen in his saloon on the night of November 19, 1895 and were left badly bruised; about 1 a.m. on November 20 Allen fired three shots into the air from the sidewalk outside to get rid of two quarrelsome men, and on November 21 Judge Peabody fined Sullivan $200 and Dempsey $50 for disturbing the peace.

Tom Allen was assaulted at his place, 619 Market Street, at about 2:30 a.m. on Friday, May 15, 1896, when two men jumped on him and a revolver was fired; Robert Flannigan and Edward Clancy were arrested and sent to Police Court.

On 27 April 1897 Tom Allen fired a revolver in the street and was arrested for disturbing the peace and carrying concealed weapons; on 30 April his cases before Judge Peabody were dismissed on payment of costs.
After William C. Brown was assaulted across the street from Tom Allen's place in July 1897 and died, Tom Allen and his housekeeper Mrs. Mary Duffy were summoned before Chief Desmond.
On 1 July 1898 several shots were fired during an attack on Tom Allen, and none of them hit him.
Tom Allen shot Timothy Confoy in his saloon on Market Street in the early hours of Sunday 26 February 1899; Confoy died that night at City Hospital, and John Spencer was wounded in the hand.

After the shooting Tom Allen was taken into custody, held at the Four Courts holdover, and a coroner's jury on 28 February 1899 returned a verdict of justifiable homicide; he was then charged with second-degree murder and released on bond.
A grand jury indicted Tom Allen for the murder of Tim Confoy on 3 May 1899; he was admitted to bond of $5,000 in Judge Klein's court, with Thomas J. Rowe going bond.
The state dismissed the murder case against Tom Allen for the killing of Timothy Confoy in Judge Fisher's court, the evidence being insufficient.
Police arrested Jesse Carraher, a musician employed in the saloon, on 3 March 1901, pending investigation of a fall.
In March 1903 Tom Allen made a will at the Baptist hospital leaving the balance of his property to Tillie Hartgrove, with $10 each to his two sisters.
Allen's daughter, Mrs. Mary Taylor, was refused access to her father, and she took her case to attorney Frank A. C. MacManus, an old friend of her father, to gain access to him.
Public Administrator Garrard Strode took charge of Tom Allen's estate in April 1903, which was in a muddled condition.
Gillespie tried to take Tom Allen's saloon from Murphy with a policeman's help, but the policeman refused to interfere and advised a warrant instead of an arrest.
Friends of Tom Allen planned to apply to the probate court on 6 April 1903 for a conservator for him.
Gillespie said he had a claim against Tom Allen for goods sold to him.
On 6 April 1903 Mrs. Mary Taylor, Tom Allen's daughter, said she would apply to the courts that day to protect her father's property and would contest the will.
Tillie Hartgrove had a writ of replevin issued at Clayton for a driving horse, and Constable Fred Lenz failed to replevin it on 21 April 1903.
In May 1903 Circuit Judge Taylor refused Tillie Hartgrove a divorce from her husband, Martin Hartgrove, after learning she had been Tom Allen's housekeeper.
Tom Allen's estate had dwindled almost to nothing and was still in litigation in May 1903.
In July 1903 Allen's widow, who lives in England, demanded a dower interest in his estate, valued at $279.80, and engaged St. Louis attorney F. H. Sullivan to bring suit against the will.
In July 1903 Hartgrove and Gillespie left Clayton threatening to replevin a hat.
Public Administrator Garrard Strode filed the inventory of Tom Allen's estate in probate court on 28 July 1903, valuing the estate, including his saloon, at $279.80.
